name: Razorpay
summary: Razorpay's engineering interviews usually include a coding or machine coding round and, for experienced roles, system design, where payments correctness (idempotency, retries, reconciliation) is a common theme. Razorpay says its interview process is closely tied to its six core values, and its careers page describes rounds on role fit, ways of working ('Synergy') and using AI in your work ('AI Edge').
looks_for: Using AI well in everyday work, which its careers page calls the 'AI Edge'

questions.text: Tell me about a production issue you owned. What did you change afterwards?
covers: What broke, who it affected and how you found out
Your part in fixing it, step by step
What you changed afterwards: alerts, tests or process, so it didn't recur

questions.text: How would you design a payment retry system that never charges a customer twice?
covers: An idempotency key per payment attempt, stored with its result
Checking the payment's status with the bank before retrying a timed-out call
Retry limits and backoff, and reconciliation to catch and refund any duplicate
Something specific: the businesses it serves or a product you'd work on
How your experience fits payments or fintech
Which value you relate to, with a short example

questions.text: Tell me about a time you challenged the way your team had always done something.
covers: The old way and what it cost
How you made the case, with data, and handled pushback
What changed and the result

questions.text: Describe a time you shared bad news early with a customer or your team. Why then?
covers: The bad news and why it was tempting to wait
How and when you shared it, and with what plan
How people responded, and what being open made possible

questions.text: Tell me about a time you had to move fast without cutting a corner that mattered.
covers: The deadline and the corner that was tempting to cut
How you kept speed while protecting what mattered, such as data or money
The outcome

questions.text: What is an idempotency key, and how would you use one in a payments API?
covers: The idea: the same request sent twice gives the same result once
Client sends a key; server stores the key with the response and returns it on a repeat
Two copies arriving at once, how long to keep keys, and which requests need one

questions.text: How would you design webhooks that tell merchants about payment events reliably?
covers: Delivery at least once, with retries and backoff when the merchant's server fails
Signed payloads and event IDs so merchants can verify and ignore duplicates
Monitoring failures, and a way for merchants to see and replay missed events

questions.text: How would you build daily reconciliation between your payment records and a bank's settlement file?
covers: Matching records by transaction ID and amount
Sorting mismatches: missing on one side, wrong amount, arriving a day late
Alerts, a review queue for people to resolve the rest, and an audit trail

questions.text: UPI success rates for one bank drop sharply at noon. What do you do?
covers: Confirming it on dashboards and isolating it to the bank, not your own systems
Reducing the impact: informing merchants, a status page, other payment options
Following up with the partner afterwards and recording what happened

questions.text: Why should money be stored as whole numbers in the smallest unit, such as paise, rather than as floating-point numbers?
covers: Floating-point numbers can't hold many decimal amounts exactly, so totals drift
Integers in paise, or a decimal type, keep sums exact
Where rounding still happens (fees, taxes, currency conversion) and how to handle it

questions.text: Walk me through how you use AI tools in your everyday work, and how you check what they produce.
covers: Two or three concrete tasks where it saves you time
How you check its output: tests, reviews, reading the code yourself
Where you choose not to use it, such as with secrets or customer data

questions.text: A small online seller gave up halfway through setting up payments. How would you improve onboarding for sellers like them?
covers: Finding where sellers drop off and why, from data and calls
Simplifying steps: documents, plain language, saving progress
Measuring time to first payment received

questions.text: Which Razorpay product would you most like to work on, and what do you know about the businesses that use it?
covers: A specific product, such as payments, payouts or business banking
Who uses it and what problem it solves for them
What you'd want to improve or learn there

tips: Payments care about correctness: talk about idempotency, retries and failure modes.
Razorpay says its interviews check for its six core values; prepare a short story for each, especially Customer First and Transparency.
Its careers page lists 'AI Edge' rounds on using AI in your work; bring a concrete example, including how you checked the output.
In design rounds, walk through failure cases out loud: timeouts, duplicate requests, a bank that replies late.
Know how a UPI or card payment flows between customer, merchant, payment gateway and bank before you go in.
